name: OpenVINO GenAI
notable_features: Continuous batching inside the library itself, with prefix caching that reuses KV cache fragments across repeated queries — and it is actually used, by OpenVINO Model Server for LLM serving.
Speculative decoding with two models of different sizes where the large model periodically corrects the small one.
KV cache token eviction: prunes low-impact tokens to shrink the cache.
Sparse attention for prefill in two modes, Tri-shape and XAttention.
Runs on OpenVINO Runtime's CPU, GPU and NPU devices with the same code — the LLMPipeline device string is 'CPU' or 'GPU' with no other change.
Multi-LoRA for text, image and video: load many adapters, select active ones per generation, blend with alpha coefficients.
Beyond LLM text: VLM, Diffusers image generation (SD, Flux), video (LTX), Whisper ASR, SpeechT5 TTS, embeddings and text rerank for RAG.
Self-contained: no external dependencies needed to run generative models, since tokenization is bundled via openvino-tokenizers.
hardware_caveats: The whole point is Intel: CPU, Intel GPU and NPU. OpenVINO Runtime's platform support matrix (linked as system-requirements for the current 2026 release) defines what actually works; there is no CUDA or ROCm path.

Models must be exported to OpenVINO IR first, via optimum-cli export openvino (documented in the quickstart). Quantization is baked in at export (the quickstart shows --weight-format int4), so precision changes are an export-time decision.

CPU-only inference is the primary target and the docs describe it as friendly to PC and laptop execution — but throughput on CPU is fundamentally bandwidth-bound, so expect single-digit tok/s for larger models regardless of optimization method.
Device string must match the model: the pipeline is constructed with a device ('CPU', 'GPU', 'NPU') and the model must have been compiled/optimized for it.
best_for: Intel Xeon, Core Ultra and Arc hardware where you want a vendor-supported engine rather than a community fork.
Intel NPU deployment — this is one of the few engines with a first-class NPU story alongside ONNX Runtime's QNN path.
Getting the largest model you can onto a PC without a discrete GPU, using int4 weight-only export plus speculative decoding.
Prefix-heavy workloads (system prompts, few-shot, repeated documents) where the prefix cache actually pays.
Serving many users on Intel hardware: the continuous batching here is real, not aspirational.
avoid_for: Maximum tok/s per GPU on any vendor.
Flexible runtime quantization switching — precision is fixed at export.
notes: scheduling claims continuous-batching and prefix-cache because the README states OpenVINO GenAI implements a continuous batching approach with prefix caching, and states it is used within OpenVINO Model Server. The distinction matters: the library provides the capability, OVMS is the serving front. Whether the in-process pipeline uses batching without OVMS in front is not stated — if that distinction matters to a reader, verify against doc/dynamic.md or the OVMS docs. Backend naming: 'intel-gpu' and 'npu' are recorded generically rather than as gpu-specific entries since OpenVINO abstracts the device; the honest mapping is 'the accelerator OpenVINO Runtime enumerates', which on Intel means Arc iGPU/dGPU and Core Ultra NPU.
